paragraphs.heading: Fish on the move
paragraphs.text: Fish migration is the movement of large numbers of fish from one place or body of water to another. These trips are bigger and last longer than the ordinary comings and goings of daily life, and they often involve whole schools. Some happen every day and others once a year or less often. They usually serve feeding or breeding, though sometimes nobody knows why the fish go.

paragraphs.heading: Words for the routes
paragraphs.text: Fish that travel between the sea and fresh water are called diadromous, from Greek words meaning through and running. Anadromous fish, such as salmon and striped bass, live as adults in the sea and swim into fresh water to spawn. Catadromous fish, such as freshwater eels, do the reverse. Amphidromous fish also cross between fresh and salt water, but not to breed: they arrive as larvae, grow into juveniles and then go back to where they started for the rest of their lives.

paragraphs.heading: Up, down and along
paragraphs.text: The bull shark can pass freely between fresh and salt water. Many ocean fish make a daily up-and-down trip, coming up to the surface at night to feed and dropping deeper during the day. Tuna shift north and south through the year, following changes in water temperature. The longest freshwater migration is made by the dourada catfish, which swims 5,500 kilometres up the Amazon.

paragraphs.heading: The forage fish triangle
paragraphs.text: Forage fish often travel far between grounds for spawning, feeding and raising young. A single stock usually loops around a triangle linking the three. One herring stock spawns off southern Norway, feeds near Iceland and uses northern Norway as its nursery. These loops may matter because feeding fish cannot recognise their own young, so moving on keeps them from eating them. Ocean currents and seasonal food supplies also shape the routes.

paragraphs.heading: Capelin around Iceland
paragraphs.text: Capelin are forage fish of the smelt family living in the Atlantic and Arctic. In summer they graze on thick swarms of plankton along the edge of the ice. Around Iceland, maturing capelin head north to feed in spring and summer and come back between September and November. Their spawning run then begins north of Iceland in December or January. In 2009 Icelandic researchers reported using a model of interacting particles to correctly predict the 2008 spawning route.

paragraphs.heading: Fish that cross borders
paragraphs.text: Some ocean travellers are called highly migratory species under Article 64 of the UN treaty on the Law of the Sea. The treaty gives no working definition but lists them in an annex: tunas, marlin, swordfish, sailfish, oceangoing sharks, dolphins and others. They are pelagic, meaning they mostly live in open water away from the sea floor. Their journeys take them both inside the 200-nautical-mile exclusive economic zones of nations and out onto the high seas, and the treaty treats them differently from other fish.

paragraphs.heading: Why people care
paragraphs.text: The fishing industry watches migration patterns closely. In rivers, fish often swim upstream to spawn, and dams are increasingly blocking these age-old routes.
